Globe Metal Industries Sramik Union Multipurpose Co-operative Society Ltd ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Asharaf Ali and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule is issued at the instance of the petitioner directing the opposite party Nos. 1-5 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 22-8-1993 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka rejecting the application of non-judicial Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1989 should not be set aside. 

 2. The facts relevant to disposal of the Rule, in short, are that, one Mr Tajul Islam Bhuiyan as General Secretary of Globe Metal Industries filed an application before, the Registrar, Co-operative Society alleging that the property described in 'ka' Schedule was declared abandoned by Government and illegally leased out to the President and Secretary, Labour Union of Globe Metal Industries for 99 years on 10-11-78. District Co-operative Officer being opposite party No. 3 observed that since the dispute involved complicated question of fact and law, he referred the matter to the District Judge, Dhaka, according to section 89 of the Co-operative Societies Ordinance, 1984. The District Judge transferred the matter to the learned Additional District Judge after registering the case as non- judicial Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1989. The learned Additional District Judge after hearing both the parties allowed the petition dated 29-3-92 of opposite party No. 1 and rejected the non-judicial Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1989. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the aforesaid order the present petitioner preferred this application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule. 

 3. Mr Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submitted that the District Co-operative Officer has power to settle the dispute unless the same is filed before the Registrar under section 86 of the Co-operative Societies Ordinance, 1984 and if so filed before the Registrar and District Officer is empowered by the Registrar to do so according to section 87(b) of the said Ordinance. He further submitted that section 89 of the said Ordinance is clear about the matter who is empowered to refer the dispute to the District Judge. He further submitted that the power of the Registrar has already been delegated to District Co-operative Officer (Annexure-M of the affidavit-in-opposition) and that when a reference is made the District Judge has got no authority to see about the legality of filing the reference and that his duty is only to decide the matter. Before reference of this case to the District Judge, a suit was filed by the petitioner in the Court being Title Suit No. 2634/1985 in the Munsif Court Dhaka. Since the suit is barred under section 133 of the Co-operative Ordinance the same has been withdrawn. Thereafter the petitioner has filed the petition before the District Co-operative Officer. It appears from Annexure-A that when the reference was first sent by the District Co-operative Officer to the District Judge, the reference was returned on the plea that the same has not been filed by the Registrar according to section 89 of the Co-operative Ordinance. Again, the District Co-operative Officer informed the District Judge that he has got power to send the reference. The District Judge received it. In Annexure-A it is found that the District Co-operative Officer has been given power except 'Ka' schedule. But in this Annexure-A a vague power has been given to the District Co-operative Officer. The sections 86, 87 and 89 of the Co-operative Ordinance, 1984 give us a clear view in the matter and those read as follows: 

 (a) stay the proceedings and refer the case to the District Judge for decision whereupon the decision of the District Judge shall be final; or 

 (b) call upon one of the parties to institute a regular suit in a civil Court for decision of the case within a period not exceeding six months to be fixed by himself and stay the proceedings in the meanwhile, if no such suit is instituted within the period so fixed, the Registrar shall pass such order as he deems fit." 

 5. Mr NH Khandkar, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party, submits that any past member or officer cannot submit petition to the Registrar regarding the affairs of Co-operative according to section 86 of the Ordinance and that Mr Tazul Islam was Secretary of the Society in 1973 and at the time of filing of this petition he was not a Secretary and, as such, his petition cannot be considered as petition according to section 86. He further submitted that since Tajul Islam as plaintiff filed a suit on behalf of the society in the civil Court and in that suit he prayed for withdrawal of the suit and the court dismissed the suit, so he is debarred from filing the petition. There is nothing in the Co-operative Ordinance, 1984 that any person of the society who filed a suit in the civil Court about any dispute is debarred from filing any petition before the Registrar of Co-operative Societies. Moreover, there is no bar by past members to file any petition regarding the affairs of society to the Registrar as according to the Ordinance any, past or present member or officer can file such petition. The petitioner being the past member of the society has right to file such petition according to section 86 of the Ordinance, 1984. In this respect I find no substance in the argument put forwarded by the learned Advocate for the petitioner. In the instant case the only question is that, whether District Co-operative Officer, has got power to entertain this petition and refer the matter to the District Judge. According to Annexure-A District Co-operative Officer who is Assistant Registrar, has been delegated all power of the Registrar except schedule one. Annexure 'F' clearly shows that the District Co-operative Officer can settle the dispute under section 86 and against the settlement Deputy Registrar will hear appeal. Annexure 'E' shows that the petitioner filed an application about the allegation of Globe Metal Industries Co-operative Societies to the District Co-Operative Officer and not to the Registrar as per section 86 of the Ordinance. According to section 86 of the Ordinance, such petition must be filed before the Registrar and according to section 87 the Registrar will refer the matter to the District Co-operative Officer for disposal. Here in this case District Co-operative Officer acted as Registrar in receiving the petition. Moreover, when the matter was referred to the District Judge for disposal by the District Co-operative Officer and the Additional District Judge's Court heard the matter and found that the petitioner filed a suit before the Court and in that suit he prayed for withdrawal, the same suit was dismissed, subject to payment of cost of Taka 150.00 and since the petitioner did not abide by the court's order he has no right to file this application. The learned Additional District Judge further observed the petitioner has filed a petition by false representation as Secretary of the Society although he is not a Secretary of the Society and, as such, there is no cause of action of this petition. Accordingly, he rejected the petition as referred to by the District Co-operative Officer. Mr NH Khandaker, Advocate for the opposite party, submitted that the reference is a non-judicial matter and in such case the Code of Civil Procedure is not applicable as there is nothing in the Ordinance about it and, as such, revisional application under section 115 CPC does not lie in this case. Admittedly impugned order was passed in a non judicial case referred to by the District Co-operative Officer according to the Co-operative Societies Ordinance, 1984. There is nothing in the Ordinance that in deciding a matter the District Judge will apply the procedure of Code of Civil Procedure. So this matter is to be decided by the District Judge according to the aforesaid Ordinance and subsequent circulars given by the Government. 

 "115. Revision. (1) The High Court may call for the record of any case which has been decided by any court subordinate to High Court Division and in which no appeal lies thereto, and if such subordinate court appears 

 the High Court may make such order in the case as it thinks fit. 

 2) The District Court may exercise the powers conferred on the High Court by sub-section (1) in respect of any case decided by a Court subordinate to such District Court in which no appeal lies and the amount or value of the subject matter whereof does not exceed the limits of the appellate jurisdiction of the District Court. 

 3) If an application under sub-section (1) in respect of a case, within the competence of the District Court has been made either to the High Court or the District Court, no further such application shall be made to either of them. 

 6. According to the above fact of CPC, when a case is decided by the court subordinate to High Court and against that decision no appeal lies, the High Court has jurisdiction to interfere with the decision of the subordinate court in its revisional jurisdiction. In the instant matter District Judge is not the court in deciding the matter under High Court. The impugned order was passed by the district Judge in a non-judicial matter in his administrative capacity and not as a court. When the District Judge does not give any decision as subordinate court to the High Court, the High Court Division has got no jurisdiction to interfere with that decision. In this respect I find substance in the submission made by the learned Advocate for the opposite party. So the application under section 115 of Code of Civil Procedure against the impugned order does not lie and, as such, the present revisional application is misconceived.
